title: Shorten the warm-up tax before serious scoring runs
summary: If early runs consistently underperform the settled part of the session, the player is paying a warm-up tax that burns good reps before quality is high enough.
why: Long warm-up ramps make peak performance harder to reach inside short practice blocks.
A predictable pre-routine is usually more valuable than adding more random warm-up volume.
actions: Build a fixed 5-10 minute opener with one easy tracking drill, one click-timing drill, and one scenario near your target task.
Do not start score attempts until movement quality and commit timing both feel stable for two consecutive runs.
If the first serious run is still weak, trim variety before adding duration.
avoid: Do not solve warm-up tax by endlessly grinding low-focus runs.
Avoid changing sensitivity or posture during the warm-up unless something is clearly wrong.

drills.reason: A fixed opener lowers run-to-run variance better than improvising the warm-up every session.

evidence.claim: Warm-up tax is best addressed with a fixed opener instead of more random warm-up volume.
